idiom_name: case/in pattern matching with deconstruct and deconstruct_keys (Ruby 3.0+)
implementation_notes: Ruby 3.0 added pattern matching as case/in: array and find patterns call deconstruct, hash patterns call deconstruct_keys, and class patterns such as Point[x:, y:] combine both, so a domain object opts into matching by defining those two methods (Struct already provides them). There is no compiler and no static coverage check: a case/in with no matching pattern and no else raises NoMatchingPatternError at run time, which is fail-fast but late, and adding an else clause removes even that safety net. Prefer case/in to case/when chains when destructuring structure, keep the else branch raising so a new variant fails loudly, and use a type checker's bottom-type helper (for example Sorbet's T.absurd) if the payloads are union-typed.
code_sketch:
Point = Struct.new(:x, :y)            # provides deconstruct + deconstruct_keys

case event
in {type: 'click', x:, y:}            # hash pattern, symbol keys only
  move(x, y)
in {type: 'key', rune:}
  handle_key(rune)
else
  raise ArgumentError, "unhandled event: #{event[:type]}"
end
pitfalls: A case/in without an else raises NoMatchingPatternError for an unmatched subject, so a rescue around it can hide genuine coverage gaps; failing loudly is usually the point.
deconstruct must return an Array and deconstruct_keys a Hash with symbol keys, otherwise the pattern raises instead of simply not matching.
Hash patterns ignore extra keys and only match symbol keys, so a shape mismatch can look like a successful structural match.
